scenes.heading: Intermolecular forces
scenes.say: Why does rain bead on a waxed car? Why does honey pour slowly? And why does water boil at one hundred degrees? It's all down to the attractions between molecules.
scenes.caption: Why does rain bead on a waxed car? Why does honey pour slowly? And why does water boil at 100 °C? It's all down to the attractions between molecules.

scenes.heading: Between, not inside
points: Covalent bonds: a few hundred kJ mol⁻¹
Boiling separates molecules, doesn't break them
scenes.say: Intermolecular forces act between molecules, and they're much weaker than the bonds inside them. When water boils, no O H bonds break. The molecules just separate. That's why water's enthalpy of vaporisation is only forty point seven kilojoules per mole, compared with about nine hundred and twenty to break its O H bonds.
scenes.caption: Intermolecular forces act between molecules, and they're much weaker than the bonds inside them. When water boils, no O–H bonds break. The molecules just separate. Water's enthalpy of vaporisation is only 40.7 kJ mol⁻¹, compared with about 920 kJ mol⁻¹ to break its O–H bonds.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: A Mexican wave: one section stands, so the next one does too
scenes.science: An instantaneous dipole induces a dipole in its neighbour
scenes.breaks: a Mexican wave moves neatly in one direction, but instantaneous dipoles flicker randomly all the time.
scenes.say: London dispersion forces are like a Mexican wave at the M C G. Electrons briefly bunch up on one side, creating an instantaneous dipole. That makes the neighbour's electrons shift too, and the two attract. A bigger crowd makes a bigger wave, so more electrons mean stronger dispersion forces. That's why iodine is a solid but fluorine is a gas.
scenes.caption: London dispersion forces are like a Mexican wave at the MCG. Electrons briefly bunch up, creating an instantaneous dipole. That induces a dipole in the neighbour, and the two attract. More electrons mean stronger dispersion forces. That's why I₂ is a solid but F₂ is a gas.

scenes.heading: Hydrogen bonds need FON
points: H bonded to F, O or N
Attracted to a lone pair on F, O or N
scenes.say: A hydrogen bond is an extra strong dipole–dipole attraction. It needs H bonded to F, O or N, attracted to a lone pair on another F, O or N. That's why water boils at one hundred degrees, while the bigger H two S boils at minus sixty.
scenes.caption: A hydrogen bond is an extra strong dipole–dipole attraction. It needs H bonded to F, O or N, attracted to a lone pair on another F, O or N. That's why water boils at 100 °C, while the bigger H₂S boils at −60 °C.

scenes.heading: Worked example: ranking boiling points
scenes.question: Rank CH₄, CH₃OH, CH₃Cl and C₂H₆ by increasing boiling point.
scenes.say: First identify the forces. Methane and ethane have only dispersion, and ethane has more electrons. Chloromethane adds a permanent dipole. Methanol is smaller, but it hydrogen bonds. So the order is methane, ethane, chloromethane, then methanol, at sixty-five degrees.
scenes.caption: First identify the forces. CH₄ and C₂H₆ have only dispersion, and C₂H₆ has more electrons. CH₃Cl adds a permanent dipole. CH₃OH is smaller, but it hydrogen bonds. So the order is CH₄ < C₂H₆ < CH₃Cl < CH₃OH (65 °C).

scenes.heading: Stronger forces mean…
scenes.say: Stronger intermolecular forces raise the boiling point, enthalpy of vaporisation, viscosity and surface tension. Vapour pressure is the odd one out. It goes down, because fewer molecules can escape the surface.

points: IMFs are much weaker than bonds
Dispersion grows with electrons and contact
Big molecules: dispersion can win (HI > HCl)
scenes.say: Quick recap. For similar-sized molecules, ion–dipole beats hydrogen bonding, then dipole–dipole, then dispersion. But for big molecules, dispersion can win. And remember: like dissolves like. Now try the practice questions!
